q: A new crew member asks which control keeps the radio quiet between calls without cutting anyone out. What do you show them?
a: The squelch, set just past the point where the hiss stops
o: The volume, turned right down until it is silent
The power switch, set to low power, 1 W
The dual watch button, so it listens less
why: Squelch mutes background hiss; set just past the hiss so weak stations still open it.

q: A friend says he called you twice this afternoon, but you heard nothing. What is the most likely reason?
a: The squelch is so high that weaker signals cannot open it
o: The 25 W setting drowns out stations that call you
Half volume mutes stations more than 5 miles away
Channel 16 stays silent unless DSC is switched on
why: Squelch turned right up cuts out everything but strong signals; back it off to just past the hiss.

fig.title: Your VHF since lunch
lines: Not a sound for three hours

q: Your friend's yacht does not answer. What do you change first?
a: Switch to high power, 25 W, and call again
o: Turn the squelch up and call again on 1 W
Stay on 1 W and call again straight away
Switch to dual watch and call again on 1 W
why: Low power, 1 W, is for short range; at 12 miles you need 25 W.

fig.title: Calling a friend
lines: Her yacht: 12 miles away, open water

q: You expect calls from the marina on its working channel and from your friend on 72, and you must keep listening to 16. Which function do you use?
a: Tri-watch: 16 plus the two channels you choose
o: Dual watch on 16 and channel 72 only
Low power with the squelch turned fully up
Channel 70 set to receive voice calls
why: Tri-watch checks 16 and two other channels in turn; dual watch covers only one besides 16.

q: The marina says your calls arrive as "…is Aurora, OVER" — the start is always missing. What are you doing wrong?
a: Speaking the instant you press; pause a moment, then speak
o: Holding the microphone a hand's width from your mouth
Calling with the squelch set too low on your own set
Transmitting on 25 W instead of 1 W so close by
why: The set needs a moment after you press the button; words spoken at once are clipped.

q: Your crew calls the marina, shouting with the microphone pressed to his lips. The marina cannot understand him. What do you tell him?
a: Hold it a few centimetres away and speak in a normal voice
o: Hold it at arm's length and shout a little louder
Keep it at his lips but switch to high power, 25 W
Keep it at his lips and turn the squelch down
why: Shouting into a mic held at the lips distorts speech; a few centimetres and a normal voice is clearest.

q: The marina complains that someone has blocked its working channel for ten minutes. Then you notice the scene in the figure. What is happening?
a: The handheld's transmit button is pressed in the locker
o: The fixed set is relaying 16 onto the marina channel
Low power on the fixed set leaks onto other channels
The handheld's low battery makes it send a carrier
why: A jammed press-to-talk button transmits non-stop and blocks the channel for everyone.

fig.title: In the cockpit
lines: Jammed in a locker under fenders
You hear nothing from the marina

q: Your charter yacht has its VHF antenna on the pushpit rail, not at the masthead. What do you expect compared with a masthead antenna?
a: Shorter range, because the antenna is much lower
o: Longer range, because the cable to the set is shorter
The same range, as height does not matter on VHF
Better range on 16 but shorter on working channels
why: VHF range depends mainly on antenna height; a low antenna sees a closer horizon.

q: Your radio checks now reach only a mile or two. What do you do?
a: Clean or replace the connector before relying on the set
o: Switch to low power to protect the set from damage
Turn the squelch to minimum to hear stations better
Use channel 70 by voice, as it carries further
why: A corroded antenna connection loses most of the signal; fix the coax and connectors.

fig.title: After the winter
lines: Antenna cable joint at the mast foot

q: You call the coast station and it reports your signal as weak. What do you do first?
a: Run the engine to charge the battery, then call again
o: Lower the antenna, as you are too close to the station
Turn your own squelch up and call again at once
Switch to channel 70 and repeat the call by voice
why: A fixed set needs a healthy supply; at low voltage it cannot transmit at full power.

lines: Engine off since yesterday, fridge running

q: You are 20 miles offshore and need to reach the coast station. You have the fixed set with a masthead antenna and a handheld. Which do you use?
a: The fixed set: more power and a much higher antenna
o: The handheld: it is closer to your mouth and clearer
The handheld, held up as high as you can in the cockpit
Either: both reach the same distance on channel 16
why: A masthead antenna and 25 W reach far beyond a handheld's few miles.

q: You are going ashore in the dinghy for the afternoon. The handheld shows one bar of battery. What do you do?
a: Charge it or fit a charged battery pack before you leave
o: Take it as it is — one bar lasts a whole afternoon
Take it on scan mode, which uses less battery
Leave it aboard and rely on someone's mobile phone
why: Transmitting drains a handheld fast; one bar may die when you press the button.

q: Your handheld is marked IPX7. What may you rely on?
a: It survives a short dunking, about 1 m for 30 minutes
o: It floats if it is dropped over the side
It can be used under water to about 10 m
It needs no fresh-water rinse after spray
why: IPX7 means protected against brief immersion; it does not mean it floats.

q: The marina is about 6 miles away over open water. How do you give the handheld its best chance?
a: Stand up on deck, high power, antenna straight up
o: Go below to the chart table, out of the wind
Stay in the cockpit and switch to low power
Hold it flat with the antenna aimed at the marina
why: Range comes from height and a vertical antenna; cabin and cockpit coamings block the signal.

fig.title: Handheld only
lines: Called from the cockpit: no reply

q: You want to check that the radio on your new charter yacht works. How do you do it?
a: Ask the marina or another boat for a check on a working channel
o: Call "radio check, all stations" on 16 at low power
Make a short voice call on channel 70 to all ships
Call "radio check, all stations" on 16 at high power
why: Radio checks go on a working channel, never on 16 or 70.

q: You switch on the fixed VHF before leaving and the display stays blank. What do you check first?
a: The VHF breaker on the switch panel and the battery switch
o: The antenna cable connector at the top of the mast
The squelch, in case it is turned fully up
The DSC settings, in case the MMSI is missing
why: No display means no power: check the breaker, fuse and battery switch before anything else.

q: The antenna cable is unplugged from the set while you fix the connector. Your crew wants to press the button "just to test it". What do you say?
a: No — transmitting without an antenna can damage the set
o: Fine on low power, 1 W, for a few seconds
Fine, as long as it is on channel 16
Fine — it simply transmits a shorter range
why: With no antenna the power has nowhere to go and can damage the transmitter.

q: You are about to abandon ship into the liferaft. The fixed VHF and a charged waterproof handheld are aboard. Which radio goes with you?
a: The waterproof handheld, kept in the grab bag or on you
o: The fixed set, unplugged and wrapped in a bin bag
Neither: the liferaft has its own radio built in
The fixed set's handset, unplugged from the set
why: Only a handheld works away from the boat's antenna and batteries.

q: You call the marina from the helm in a strong wind. They hear mostly a roar. What do you do?
a: Shield the microphone from the wind and speak normally
o: Shout louder with the microphone held further away
Switch to high power so the voice cuts through
Turn the squelch down so your voice opens it
why: Wind across the microphone drowns speech; shelter it with your hand or body.

q: Which pair can usually talk over the longest distance?
a: A yacht's masthead set and a coast station on a hill
o: Two yachts, each with a masthead antenna
A handheld in a cockpit and a masthead set
Two handhelds, each held up in a cockpit
why: Range grows with the height of both antennas; a hilltop coast station sees furthest.
